title: Keep the names
hookLine: good, modest, truthful, even-minded: keep these names and deserve them (Meditations 10.8)

cards: A name tag at a conference. A title in an email signature. Mom, coach, nurse, friend.
Names do work: they tell people what to expect from us, and they quietly tell us what to expect from ourselves.
In book ten Marcus picks out a short list of names he wants to answer to, and then he tells himself something harder. Don't just wear them. Deserve them.

teach.b: Once you've taken these names, Marcus writes, good, modest, truthful, rational, even-minded, high-minded, take care not to trade them for others. And if you lose them, come back to them quickly. He defines three of them.
Rational means paying attention: looking at each thing carefully, not carelessly.
Even-minded means accepting willingly what the nature of the whole hands you. High-minded means lifting your mind above the body's pleasures and pains, above shabby fame, and above death.
Hold on to the names, he says, without wanting other people to call you by them. A name you live by is different from a name you're given.
The coach who's called coach but never shows up has the name and not the thing. Then a hard picture.

teach.h: THE ARENA, AND THE QUIET CORNER.
teach.b: Going on as before, torn and stained, Marcus says, is like the fighters in the arena, half eaten by wild beasts, covered in wounds and blood, still begging to be kept until tomorrow, only to be thrown again to the same claws.

It's a brutal image, and he turns it on himself: fix yourself in these few names, he says, and stay in them. And if you feel yourself slipping, go off bravely to some quiet corner where you can hold on to them again.

how: Some readers of the Meditations choose one of Marcus's names each morning, truthful or even-minded, say, and return to it during the day whenever they notice they've let it slip.

o: a sports field where friends compete
a stage where you perform for applause
Marcus's image for going on torn, as before

games.q: keep the names — tap the pairs.
p: accepting what the whole hands you
above pleasure, pain, fame and death

s: Marcus wants other people to call him good
he says hold the names without wanting others to call you by them.
he defines rational as paying careful attention
looking at each thing carefully, not carelessly.

games.q: you've slipped, and been anything but even-minded all morning. you're Marcus. what now?
o: drop the name; clearly it isn't you.
come back to it quickly, maybe in a quiet corner.
games.why: if you lose the names, he writes, return to them quickly; if you're slipping, go off to some corner where you can hold them again.

practice: Hear the six names: good, modest, truthful, rational, even-minded, high-minded. Let the one you'd most like to deserve today stand out, not the one you're best at, the one you need.
Picture one moment ahead where you'll need it, a meeting, a conversation, a temptation, and see yourself answering to that name there.

wordCard.voice: Arena. Marcus compares going on as before to a wounded fighter in the arena, still begging to be kept until tomorrow. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a name. Marcus asks himself to keep a few names, and deserve them.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the name. A name lived, not just given. Day six hundred fifteen, done.
